doc.title: Neal Caine interviewed by Monk Rowe, New Hartford, New York, September 26, 2019

title: Playing with the time versus playing the time
summary: Discussion of modern players who play with the time; Caine likens rhythm section playing to conversation and stresses swinging first.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why

blocks.x: I’m not that informed about current creative jazz, but much of it I hear, what I have heard, sounds like the bass player and the drummer are playing with the time, playing with the time, rather than playing the time, if that makes sense.
Yeah I know what you mean.
And I find it challenging to figure out. That’ just my personal thing. But do you know what I’m talking about?

I do know what you mean. I mean you know that’s another reason this music’s so hard, because you have to learn how to play it, you have to get the tools and the technique and the songs and the sound and everything that you’re required to do it, and then you have to apply it. I mean I’m not going to name names, but we both know a lot of great musicians who are really great but you can’t stand what they’re doing. You know like it’s stupid. Or whatever. Whatever you think. Or I shouldn’t say stupid, but it’s too busy, or they’ve lost the essence of the song. I mean you have to be swinging and grooving first, and I like complex stuff, but it’s got to be applied correctly you know. I always just equate rhythm section playing to a conversation. I mean all jazz, I mean it sounds maybe Ken Burnsish but it’s true. I mean if we’re talking right now and I start talking real fast and start saying all types of crazy stuff, it doesn’t make sense. And I think that’s what you mean with these drummers’ problem.
Yeah. And if I can’t feel a pulse from somebody I guess I get uneasy.
Yeah. What’s the point? What’s the point, man.”
It don’t mean a thing if, whoever said that.
